text: Quick reference for visible external signs and their likely causes. Wattles/combs: swelling suggests Fowl Cholera (which can progress to abscessed wattles when chronic); nodules suggest Fowl Pox (typically on non-feathered areas). Eyes: watery, red, and inflamed can come from several respiratory diseases (ND, Laryngotracheitis, IB, Bird Flu, Mycoplasma) causing discomfort and rubbing rather than direct eye damage; swelling with pus-like discharge and stuck-together eyelids suggests Coryza or Mycoplasma; tumors causing blindness suggest Marek's disease. Nostril discharge: watery/clear suggests IB; sticky pus with facial swelling and labored breathing suggests Coryza; blood-tinged discharge/clots suggest ILT. Skin lesions: wart-like nodules on non-feathered head/leg areas suggest Fowl Pox; nodules at the base of leg feathers suggest Marek's disease; a soiled, irritated vent with watery droppings suggests Gumboro; rough, enlarged, infected leg scales suggest scaly leg mites (treat by soaking legs in oil or cream to suffocate the mites, every 3–4 days for 2 weeks, letting old scales fall off and be replaced). Feathers: lice eggs stuck in clusters suggest lice (treat with Carbaryl, but not on layers whose eggs are sold); poorly developed feathers or feather-picking suggest a methionine/protein deficiency (birds pull and eat feathers, which are methionine-rich, to compensate); ruffled feathers with depression are a general sign of serious illness across nearly all infectious diseases and parasite burdens (e.g. Coccidiosis); annual feather loss starting at the head is normal molting (hens typically stop laying for 6–7 weeks during this); sticky, pasted vent feathers suggest Salmonellosis. Emaciation (wasting/thinness): intestinal worms absorbing nutrients; Leukosis (lymphoid tumors, mainly in liver and spleen, also potentially ovary/lungs, with appetite loss and progressive wasting); or simply insufficient feeding, common in layers drawing on their reserves while brooding.
